question_en:
The studio recovered six institutional photographs of the same volume of an old manuscript, arranged from left to right according to the treatment workflow. Please answer the following questions:

1. In the first set of collation diagrams, which is the next surviving numbered leaf after the leaf indicated by the paper strip? What joining structure was later adopted for the single leaf shown in the image?
2. Comparing the before-and-after photographs in the second set, what was the original obvious problem on the last leaf? How was the tape removed? What materials were used to repair the damaged and missing areas respectively?
3. In the third set of photographs, how are the old binding fragments and the rebound manuscript stored respectively? How are both parts finally boxed together for return to storage?

Response format: Please answer in numbered points (1)–(3); answer all three questions in text with separate points, providing respectively the leaf sequence and joining structure, the original problems with treatment methods and materials, and the storage and joint boxing methods for both parts.
answer:
(1) Next surviving numbered leaf: folio 13; Joining structure: kozo hooked guard, standardized category leaf guard; the paper strip is adhered along the spine edge of the single leaf and sewn through the fold into the text block.

(2) Original problems: large missing areas and six small strips of pressure-sensitive tape. Tape removal: first apply a facing using kozo tissue and 2% Klucel G in ethanol on the reverse side, then mechanically separate the tape carrier with a spatula, and remove adhesive residue with a crepe eraser. Repair damaged areas with thin kozo tissue; fill missing areas with one layer of Korean chamdak paper plus one layer of thin kozo, tone with liquid acrylics, adhere with refined wheat starch paste, and finally release the facing tissue using ethanol.

(3) Old binding fragments, after necessary consolidation, are individually placed in Mylar sleeves and then positioned in a right-side four-flap cardstock enclosure; the rebound manuscript is placed in a left-side four-flap enclosure. Both inner enclosures are jointly placed in a custom cloth-covered clamshell box for return to storage.

# Detailed Simulated Retrieval Trajectory · P2-11-A01

## Step 01 · Identify the three problem areas in the current six images

Action: View the three-column photographs in the current final-image-real, first identifying the visible objects and paper strips for PAGE ORDER, LEAF TREATMENT, and FINAL HOUSING respectively.

Evidence Observation: The top image of the left group is the overall collation diagram; the bottom image shows details before and after treatment of Gathering 3, with a paper strip reading SURVIVING NOTE: 12v footer; the middle group shows before-and-after repair of the last leaf; the right group shows old binding fragments and an open storage box. The layout between photographs provides the workflow order; material names cannot be inferred solely from color or appearance.

Result of this step: Proceed by expanding the left, middle, and right groups; this question does not specify a condition of "six webpages jumping sequentially" or a threshold stop condition; completing the three groups of questions is sufficient, without constructing additional routes.

## Step 02 · Locate the LOC Rumi conservation project via photo combinations

Action: Example query: "Library of Congress Rumi manuscript conservation collation last folio rehousing". First, use combined features such as old manuscript, collation diagrams, black-background fragment photos, and double-inner-enclosure boxes to find cases from the same institution.

Evidence Observation: The LOC Rumi project homepage leads to Treatment; this project preserves a photo sequence of Examination, Treatment of the Leaves, Rebinding, and Rehousing. The current six images match the corresponding images leaves1, rebind1, leaves5, leaves6, rehouse1, and rehouse2 of that project, rather than six different projects.

Evidence Links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/index.html
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html

Result of this step: Lock onto the same manuscript case and the core treatment page. Subsequent precise conservation methods rely primarily on the captions of this page; auxiliary terminology pages do not replace this case.

## Step 03 · First image return: 12v and the next surviving numbered leaf

Action: Return from the project page to the current photo in the left group, read the paper strip 12v footer, and locate the Gathering containing 12 and the immediately following 13 in the collation diagram.

Evidence Observation: The 12v in the paper strip refers to the verso of leaf 12, not page 12 or Gathering 12. The next surviving numbered leaf after 12 in the image is 13; both the overall image and the partial view of the third gathering support this numbering relationship.

Evidence Links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/leaves1_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/rebind1_g.jpg

Result of this step: The leaf sequence part of the first question yields folio 13; subsequently verify the institution's text regarding missing leaves and single-leaf structure to prevent miswriting "next surviving leaf" as implying the text is necessarily continuous.

## Step 04 · Use collation instructions to distinguish surviving order from text loss

Action: Read the treatment page explanations regarding collation and catchwords; refer to the Folger glossary only when needing to explain the general function of catchwords.

Evidence Observation: The institution's explanation states that the catchword of 12v does not match the first word of folio 13, meaning the number of leaves missing between them is unknown. This fact does not negate that "the next surviving numbered leaf is 13"; it only restricts asserting that the original direct next leaf still survives intact.

Evidence Links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html
https://folgerpedia.folger.edu/Glossary_of_manuscript_terms

Result of this step: Write the answer as folio 13 according to the current phrasing of the question; do not write an unknown number of leaves, nor force catchword theory into another leaf sequence answer.

## Step 05 · Return to images to compare before-and-after treatment of the third gathering, then check joining names

Action: Return to the bottom image of the left group, correlate the single folium before treatment with the added joining lines after treatment; then return to the Rebinding image captions to read the specific material structure.

Evidence Observation: The caption after treatment explains that kozo hooked guards were added to the single folia, and blank kozo leaves were inserted where leaves were missing. Since the first question asks for the joining structure adopted for the single leaf, adopt kozo hooked guard; do not treat the newly added blank leaves themselves as the joining.

Evidence Links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/rebind1_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html

Result of this step: The joining structure is locked as kozo hooked guard; still need to use terminology definitions to clarify how the structure works.

## Step 06 · Verify the standard structure of leaf guards

Action: Example query: "Ligatus leaf guards single leaves spine edge". Open the saved standard concept page to correlate the project term hooked guard to the leaf guard category.

Evidence Observation: Ligatus defines leaf guards as paper strips adhered along the spine edge of a single or double leaf and incorporated into sewing through their fold. It explains the function of "guard"; the materials and form using kozo and hooked in this case still come from the LOC image captions.

Evidence Links:
https://lob.is.ed.ac.uk/concept/3616
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html

Result of this step: The first question forms two parts: leaf sequence and joining structure: folio 13; kozo hooked guard, standard category leaf guard, adhered along the spine edge and sewn through the fold into the text block.

## Step 07 · Second image return: Observe damage on the last leaf before repair

Action: Leave the left group materials, return to the current middle group top image LAST LEAF—BEFORE; compare fragmented edges, large missing areas, and long strip fragments with the same photo from the institution.

Evidence Observation: The current image shows large missing areas and breaks on the leaf, but the exact count of small pressure-sensitive tape strips should not be pretended to be counted solely from the zoomed-in photo. The LOC leaves5 caption explicitly states big losses and six small strips of pressure-sensitive tape.

Evidence Links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/leaves5_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html

Result of this step: Record "large missing areas and six small strips of pressure-sensitive tape"; among these, the tape count comes from the caption text, while visual evidence only supports the damage morphology and photo identity.

## Step 08 · First check temporary consolidation before tape removal

Action: Locate the section Before removing the tape in the same leaves5 caption, read according to the treatment sequence, and do not substitute general tape recommendations for this case's formula.

Evidence Observation: Before removing the tape, apply a facing on the reverse side of the leaf: use kozo tissue, adhered with 2% Klucel G in ethanol. This step is temporary support for damaged areas, not the final filling material for missing areas.

Evidence Links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/leaves5_g.jpg

Result of this step: Preserve the operation sequence: first add temporary facing on the reverse side, then process the tape. Record concentration, solvent, and position.

## Step 09 · Verify different removal methods for tape carrier and adhesive residue

Action: Continue reading the leaves5 caption, separating carrier and still-sticky adhesive residue; the NARA Paper-Based Records page is used only to understand the background of pressure-sensitive tape.

Evidence Observation: The institution records that the tape carrier is mechanically separated with a spatula; still-sticky adhesive residue is removed with a crepe eraser. Do not generalize to "remove tape with alcohol dissolution" just because ethanol appears in the same paragraph; that would confuse the solvent for the facing with the carrier removal action.

Evidence Links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html
https://www.archives.gov/preservation/holdings-maintenance/paper

Result of this step: Write the tape method as mechanically separating the carrier with a spatula and removing residue with a crepe eraser; maintain the sequence and functional distinction from the previous step's facing.

## Step 10 · Return to the after-repair photo in the middle group, separating tear repair from loss filling

Action: Return from the method text to the current middle group bottom image LAST LEAF—AFTER, compare with the damaged state of the same leaf above, then read the corresponding caption in leaves6.

Evidence Observation: After repair, the leaf has entered the rebound text block, and the original large missing areas have been filled. The LOC caption distinguishes that breaks and tears use thin kozo tissue; losses use one layer of Korean chamdak paper plus one layer of thin kozo. The two types of damage do not share a single generic "Japanese paper" answer.

Evidence Links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/leaves6_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html

Result of this step: Split the material part of the second question into damaged areas: thin kozo tissue; missing areas: Korean chamdak paper + thin kozo (two layers).

## Step 11 · Complete toning, adhesion, and release of temporary facing

Action: Continue reading the second half of the leaves6 caption to confirm the toning agent, final adhesive, and finishing actions.

Evidence Observation: The filling layers are toned with liquid acrylics, adhered with refined wheat starch paste; afterwards, use ethanol to release the facing tissue on the reverse side. Releasing the facing is the conclusion of temporary support and should not be miswritten as a material for tear repair or the primary removal method for the tape carrier.

Evidence Links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/leaves6_g.jpg

Result of this step: The methods and materials for the second question are complete; next, return to the right group photos to resolve separate housing and joint return to storage, without expanding into a full rebinding process list.

## Step 12 · Third image return: Storage of old binding fragments

Action: Return to the current right group top image OLD BINDING REMAINS, identify old boards, threads, and small fragmented binding materials, then locate the first photo and caption of Rehousing.

Evidence observation: The LOC caption explicitly states that the old left board and other old binding remains are placed in Mylar sleeves; the delaminated old board and remaining covering materials undergo necessary consolidation before being sleeved. The image shows the separated state of the transparent sleeves, and the specific polyester brand name Mylar is provided by the caption.

Evidence links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/rehouse1_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html

Result of this step: Recorded that old fragments are first consolidated and individually placed in Mylar sleeves; still need to check what type of inner enclosure the transparent sleeves are placed into and where the book is located.

## Step 13 · Open the storage box photo and compare the left and right parts

Action: Return to OPEN STORAGE BOX below the right group; compare with the second caption of the Rehousing photo according to the left-right orientation in the image, without swapping left and right.

Evidence observation: The caption states that Mylar sleeves are placed in the right-side four-flap cardstock enclosure; the rebound manuscript is located in the left-side four-flap enclosure. In the current input image, the right side shows a label and an enclosure, while the left side is the location of the other enclosure; both inner enclosures jointly occupy the outer box.

Evidence links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/rehouse2_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html

Result of this step: The right side preserves the transparent sleeves for old fragments, and the left side preserves the rebound manuscript; each has a four-flap inner enclosure.

## Step 14 · Verify the outermost box for joint return to storage

Action: Read the last sentence of the same Rehousing caption; use the principles for damaged components and boxing of NARA Bound Materials as background interpretation, but retain the specific construction of this LOC case.

Evidence observation: LOC explicitly states that a custom cloth-covered clamshell box houses both four-flaps together. The outermost layer is a custom cloth-covered clamshell box that simultaneously accommodates both four-flap enclosures; one cannot answer only "acid-free box" while omitting the level where both parts are preserved together.

Evidence links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/treatment.html
https://www.archives.gov/preservation/holdings-maintenance/bound

Result of this step: Complete hierarchy for question 3: fragments → Mylar sleeves → right four-flap enclosure; rebound manuscript → left four-flap enclosure; both sets → custom cloth-covered clamshell box.

## Step 15 · Review current images group by group to check the scope corresponding to the three questions

Action: Finally, return sequentially to the current photos of the left, middle, and right groups; bind each method or name to the corresponding image and caption, and check whether there is any confusion with other old version tasks.

Evidence observation: The left group addresses the next surviving numbered leaf and joining; the middle group addresses damage to the last leaf, tape, and repair/filling; the right group addresses separate enclosures for fragments and the book, and joint boxing. Folger, Ligatus, and NARA serve as auxiliary interpretations, while LOC treatment bears the precise facts for this case. Material formulas that cannot be directly read after zooming in on the images are explicitly derived from the text.

Evidence links:
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/leaves1_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/rebind1_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/leaves5_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/leaves6_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/rehouse1_g.jpg
https://www.loc.gov/preservation/conservators/rumi/detail/rehouse2_g.jpg

Result of this step: All three questions are closed. The current prompt does not require a procurement table, a count of six-page accesses, or the number of leaves with unknown succession words; none of these are added to the final answer.

## final_answer
